content: Nickel is a component of amalgam, a commonly used dental restorative material, which can cause adjacent areas of teeth to appear black or gray. Chlorhexidine, a widely used mouthwash, is known to cause yellow-brown staining near the gingival margins of teeth. Systemic disorders can also lead to tooth discoloration. For instance, congenital erythropoietic porphyria results in the deposition of porphyrins in teeth, giving them a red-brown coloration. Blue discoloration of teeth may occur in conditions such as alkaptonuria and, rarely, Parkinson's disease. Diseases like erythroblastosis fetalis and biliary atresia can cause teeth to appear green due to the deposition of biliverdin. Additionally, trauma to a tooth can result in color changes, such as pink, yellow, or dark gray. Pink and red discolorations are also observed in patients with lepromatous leprosy. Certain medications, such as tetracycline antibiotics, can integrate into the tooth structure, leading to intrinsic staining. Tooth eruption can be influenced by environmental factors. When the eruption process is prematurely halted, the tooth is considered impacted. The most common cause of tooth impaction is insufficient space in the oral cavity. Other causes include tumors, cysts, trauma, or thickened bone or soft tissue. Ankylosis occurs when a tooth, after erupting into the oral cavity, becomes fused to the alveolar bone via its cementum or dentin. This condition can result in the retention of a primary tooth instead of its replacement by a permanent tooth. Orthodontists may intentionally alter the natural progression of tooth eruption to either delay or accelerate the process for purposes such as space maintenance or to prevent crowding or spacing issues. If a primary tooth is extracted before the root of its succeeding permanent tooth has reached one-third of its total growth, the eruption of the permanent tooth will be delayed. Conversely, if the roots of the permanent tooth are more than two-thirds complete, its eruption will be accelerated. The effects on eruption speed are uncertain when the root development is between one-third and two-thirds complete. Anodontia refers to the complete absence of tooth development. Hyperdontia is the presence of more teeth than normal, while hypodontia refers to the absence of some teeth. Hypodontia typically describes the lack of development of one or more teeth, whereas oligodontia is used to describe the absence of six or more teeth. Systemic disorders associated with hyperdontia include Apert syndrome, Cleidocranial dysostosis, Crouzon syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Gardner syndrome, and Sturge-Weber syndrome. Systemic disorders linked to hypodontia include Crouzon syndrome, ectodermal dysplasia, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and Gorlin syndrome. Microdontia is a condition where teeth are smaller than normal, while macrodontia refers to teeth that are larger than usual. Microdontia is most commonly observed in maxillary lateral incisors, followed by third molars. Generalized macrodontia can occur in conditions such as pituitary gigantism and pineal hyperplasia. It may also present unilaterally in cases of hemifacial hyperplasia. Abnormalities in tooth shape include gemination, where a developing tooth partially splits into two teeth, and fusion, which is the union of two adjacent teeth during development. Concrescence refers to the fusion of two separate teeth at their cementum. Accessory cusps, such as talon cusps, cusps of Carabelli, or dens evaginatus, are additional cusps on a tooth. Dens invaginatus, also known as dens in dente, is a deep invagination in a tooth, giving the appearance of a tooth within a tooth. Ectopic enamel refers to enamel found in an unusual location, such as the root of a tooth. Taurodontism is characterized by an enlarged tooth body and pulp chamber and is associated with conditions like Klinefelter syndrome, tricho-dento-osseous syndrome, triple X syndrome, and XYY syndrome. Hypercementosis, the excessive formation of cementum, can result from trauma, inflammation, acromegaly, rheumatic fever, or Paget's disease of bone. Dilaceration is a bend in the root of a tooth, often caused by trauma during tooth formation. Supernumerary roots refer to the presence of more roots on a tooth than expected. Structural abnormalities include amelogenesis imperfecta, a condition where enamel does not form properly or at all, and dentinogenesis imperfecta, where dentin formation is defective and may be associated with osteogenesis imperfecta. Dentin dysplasia affects the roots and pulp of teeth. Regional odontodysplasia is a condition affecting enamel, dentin, and pulp, causing teeth to appear ghostly on radiographs. In animals, teeth vary significantly. Some animals, such as turtles and tortoises, are toothless, while others, like sharks, continuously replace their teeth throughout their lifetime. Walrus tusks are elongated canine teeth that grow continuously. Dogs are less prone to dental caries compared to humans due to the high pH of their saliva, which prevents enamel demineralization. Unlike humans, whose ameloblasts cease enamel production after tooth development, rodents continuously produce enamel and must gnaw on various materials to wear down their teeth. Horses have twelve premolars, twelve molars, and twelve incisors. The structure of horse teeth differs from human teeth, as their enamel and dentin layers are intertwined.
